statements.text: And in the defense industry, I'm worried because I've seen those documentaries like Terminator and Star Trek. [...] And I understand that we have the potential for systems to actually start outthinking us and actually out-reacting and has a potential to damage us.
statements.context: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing on artificial intelligence and national interest.

statements.text: Great, thanks. One thing—I'm not even sure who to ask this for, but I'll let the panel decide who's the best person. I have a real sincere concern that 100% of our AI chips right now are produced in Taiwan, with the posturing we have in China talking about they are going to take over Taiwan. Having an adversarial country owning 100% of the production of the most influential technology in world history deeply concerns me. Now, I know AMD has some processes that they want to produce AI outside of Taiwan in the next couple years, but in the meantime, what do we do? I feel like all of our eggs are in one basket. Please.
statements.context: Rep. McCormick poses a question to a witness panel at a congressional hearing on AI and national interest.

statements.text: My concern is we have an enormous amount of foreign students at our universities right now in some of the leading technology areas, including AI development. Georgia Tech is right in my back yard. I went to Georgia Tech. I did my pre-med there. And we are literally educating them and sending them right back there. That is access to leading technology in America. Is that what you are discussing when you talk about access or are you talking about in the industry itself? Or the stuff that is out on the internet? Or is it everything?
statements.context: Rep. McCormick questions a witness during a House Armed Services Committee hearing titled 'Man and Machine: Artificial Intelligence on the Battlefield.'

statements.text: We buy all of those chips you're talking about the AI chips, the leading-edge chips, all of that—none of them are made in America right now, which is why I've got to work like crazy every day to bring that manufacturing home as fast as we can.
statements.context: Senate hearing reviewing the CHIPS and Science Act one year after enactment, where Senator McCormick questions Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo about U.S. semiconductor supply vulnerability vis-à-vis Taiwan and China.

statements.text: I think the CHIPS Act kind of didn't address that fully, that we really don't have that production capability, nor do we even have a plan to—the plants aren't—haven't started being built here for the AI chips, and I'm really worried about that.
statements.context: Closing remarks at a House hearing reviewing the first year of the CHIPS and Science Act.

statements.text: Excellent. Mr. Matheny, do you believe that had the United States banned outbound investments to Chinese about 15 years ago or so would have made a different in the ultimate outcome of the advancement of AI and other technologies that are possibly harmful in the competition and strategic outcome with what we have done?
statements.context: Question posed by Rep. McCormick during a House hearing on U.S. capital flows to China's military sector.

statements.text: With that being said, though, we live in a time where real national security threats exist, and we must ensure that our universities and research systems have clear guidance to place—in place to ensure that we are safeguarding our critical research programs from foreign adversaries, specifically, the Chinese Communist Party.
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing examining federal science agency actions to secure the U.S. science and technology enterprise.

statements.text: For AI, it's about 100 percent. They produce about 90 percent of the world's AI chips, the other 10 percent in Samsung. So my point is if China has unfettered access to our technologies and now they say they're going to take the one place that we make all of our AI chips overseas, that is extremely concerning.
statements.context: U.S. House hearing on countering China, titled 'Empowering American Businesses and Denying Chinese Military Our Technology'.

statements.text: I would suggest that your bureau is also work in conjunction with us to limit that access for national security and for your own good. [...] Approximately how many AI percentage—in percentage rate IT production, how much of our AI production is produced over in Taiwan right now?
statements.context: House hearing on countering China, with a congressman pressing the Bureau of Industry and Security on technology transfer risks and Taiwan dependency.

statements.text: What challenges does this rate of acceleration—in other words, as we are trying to keep up legislatively and regulatory-wise, what does this acceleration create for integrating data, artificial intelligence, and digital solutions for the DOD and how it applies, like, just trying to keep up with this pace?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on AI and technology in DOD operations, where the member questions a witness about AI's rapid advancement and regulatory challenges.

statements.text: We are going to learn a lot with the establishment of our AI task force. We completed an AI roadmap last year, and that lays out for us the technologies that we want to begin to experiment with and pilot and introduce to our force.
statements.context: General Haugh, head of U.S. Cyber Command, responds to a question from a House Armed Services Committee member about proactive AI use during the NDAA FY2025 hearing.

statements.text: I think Taiwan is an extremely important not ally, just partner in the future of AI, which I think is going to be transformative to the entire world. [...] I think they produce about 100 percent of our AI chips, and about 90 percent of the world's AI chips. [...] China recently stated that they are going to take over Taiwan by 2027, which is worrisome to me.
statements.context: US House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing reviewing the Development Finance Corporation's efforts to compete with China's Belt and Road Initiative.

statements.text: One such technological vulnerability is the loophole in remote access to cloud computing. While the United States has banned the export of advanced semiconductor chips to companies in China, many have exploited this loophole by accessing this technology remotely via cloud technology. They, then, use this access to develop artificial intelligence technology and strengthen the Chinese military.
statements.context: Rep. McCormick speaks at a House Foreign Affairs Committee markup in support of the Remote Access Security Act, which addresses cloud-computing loopholes in chip export controls.

statements.text: And we can't power the AI revolution without cheap and reliable power for data centers and tech clusters. [...] I am putting together a Pennsylvania energy—an innovation summit later this year to bring together the energy sector, leading AI companies, huge sources of capital, and global investors to deliver on President Trump's vision to unleash American energy and technological leadership.
statements.context: Senator McCormick speaks during the Senate hearing on the nomination of Chris Wright as Secretary of Energy.

statements.text: Mr. Mattis, just very quickly, we saw all the announcements this week around DeepSeek-R1. Does the proliferation of open source AI models that are trained to push the CCP's propaganda advance the party's efforts to shape public discourse in the United States, and how can this open source approach enable future influence operations?
statements.context: Senate hearing on Chinese malign influence, featuring Senator McCormick questioning a witness about DeepSeek-R1 and open-source AI models.

statements.text: we are talking a lot today about artificial intelligence and the importance of it for our economy and for our national security. To reap the full benefits of the AI revolution, we need power. We need an expansion of natural gas production and nuclear power, in particular, to power the next generation of AI.
statements.context: Senator McCormick questions nominees during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on energy infrastructure needed to support AI.

statements.text: Both of these bills are meaningful steps forward in reducing permitting delays and helping us to win the AI race, but there is still so much work to be done.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Senator McCormick during a Senate hearing on pending grid-infrastructure legislation.

statements.text: The first is the Liquid Cooling for AI Act, which I introduced with Senator Chris Coons. This legislation is designed to help ensure American AI infrastructure is the most efficient, resilient, secure, and advanced in the world.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Senator McCormick at a Senate Energy Subcommittee hearing on pending legislation addressing grid capacity and AI infrastructure.

statements.text: As we know, data centers are crucial to winning the AI race with China. Data centers' annual energy use could grow from 4.4 percent of the country's total annual electricity consumption to 12 percent by 2028, just around the corner. [...] is the current system keeping pace with that demand, or do you see strains emerging?
statements.context: Senate hearing pending legislation, with a senator questioning a witness about data-center energy demand and grid interconnection.
